newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone army ruler maps out defiant timetable.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone army ruler maps out defiant timetable.

text.p: Sierra Leone's military ruler, Johnny Paul Koroma, mapped out a defiant timetable of more than four years to return the West African country to civilian rule.
Koroma, reading a prepared statement on state radio and television late on Wednesday, said the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council would not hold elections until the year 2001.

Sierra Leone's West African neighbours are pressing for the immediate return of ousted president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah at talks with his envoys in Ivory Coast, but Koroma called on Nigerian-led West African forces to leave the country.

"The AFRC will not be stampeded into hurrying matters beyond their appointed course," he said, adding that the junta was prepared to hand over to what he called "a properly ordered constitutional order."
"The AFRC stands ready to defend the sovereignty of Sierra Leone to the last drop of its blood," he said.

Sierra Leone's neighbours, led by regional giant Nigeria, say Kabbah, who was toppled by soldiers on May 25, must be reinstated. Rebels, who took up arms in 1991, rallied to the coup which has been widely denounced abroad.

A committee of four West African foreign ministers has been pressing for Kabbah's reinstatement through dialogue and economic sanctions but Sierra Leone's neighbours have not ruled out the military option.
Koroma made no mention of Kabbah, who took office in March 1996 after multi-party elections ending four years of army rule.

Talks in Ivory Coast's commercial capital Abidjan on Tuesday and Wednesday, the second round of meetings between the two sides to try to head off a showdown, showed no immediate sign of breaking the impasse.
"We, who are here, are still negotiating," Captain Paul Thomas, one of the original coup leaders, told Reuters in Abidjan after Korama's statement.

Koroma said parliamentary elections would take place in February 2001, elections for a state council would take place by May with presidential elections by November. He did not spell out the role of the state council.

He said a ban on political parties would be lifted at least a couple of months before the parliamentary poll. The constitution would remain suspended and a ban on political parties would remain in force until then.

Nigerian-led troops are in Sierra Leone under a pre-coup defence pact. Their attempt to dislodge the coup leaders with a June 2 naval bombardment backfired when Sierra Leone soldiers and rebels attacked exposed Nigerian positions.

On the economic front, Koroma said the impoverished country's main commercial banks -- Barclays Bank, Standard Chartered and the largely Sierra-Leone owned Union Trust Bank -- would be liquidated unless they reopened by August 4.
The foreign owners of Barclays, the market leader, and Standard Chartered have said they will remain closed until the security improves, leaving many Sierra Leonian depositors without cash.
